Match situation: Second innings / chase with constrained required scoring pace
Individual responsibility: Batter’s eligible scoring and survival opportunities.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Pressure may exist when the time-safe task is demanding; late innings alone is insufficient.
Relevant candidate observations: Required pace, balls/wickets remaining, batter-attributed runs, dismissal/boundary events, baseline.
Unresolved data requirements: Batter-faced/legal-ball classification; state timing; event attribution; thresholds and exposure.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — retain as second-innings chase case; operational state and data gates pending.
Dashboard handling: No operational label until definition and metric gates pass; show missing fields and status.

Match situation: Second innings / chase with comfortable state late in innings
Team task: Complete chase without acute scoring constraint.
Individual responsibility: Batter’s actual opportunity; role may be low urgency.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Late stage does not necessarily imply pressure; may be a useful non-pressure comparison if state rule supports it.
Relevant candidate observations: Required pace/gap, balls/wickets, eligible outcomes and role.
Unresolved data requirements: Validated state fields and comparable baseline population.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — retain as non-pressure/counterexample case where validated state supports it.
Dashboard handling: Late stage alone is not pressure; counterexample only if approved state rule supports it.

Match situation: First innings with team setting a total
Team task: Define first-innings setting-total pressure as a distinct conceptual team task; operational classification remains deferred.
Individual responsibility: Batter’s responsibility varies by entry, role and remaining resources.
Why pressure may or may not exist: The first-innings task is distinct from a chase; no chase variables transfer. Pressure may not be labeled until historical expectations, source fields/timestamps, operational rules and readiness gates are validated.
Relevant candidate observations: Score/over at event, wickets/resources, player entry, role and scoring response.
Unresolved data requirements: First-innings task/benchmark; verified event-time fields and timestamps; defensible historical expectation; approved operational rules and metric-specific readiness gates.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — distinct first-innings setting-total task; until validated and approved, opportunity remains UNCLASSIFIED or NOT CLASSIFIABLE, not non-pressure.
Dashboard handling: Keep UNCLASSIFIED/NOT CLASSIFIABLE until all specified inputs and gates are validated and approved; never relabel as non-pressure.

Team task: Preserve resources and rebuild scoring opportunity.
Individual responsibility: Batter role and partnership responsibility must be defined before event.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Wickets lost may imply constraint but a wicket alone does not prove pressure or individual responsibility.
Relevant candidate observations: Pre-event wickets, balls, score pace, entry state, partnership and individual outcomes.
Unresolved data requirements: Reliable partnership and player exposure; role definition; selection context.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — stabilization responsibility is pre-event/contextual; partnership and exposure validation pending.
Dashboard handling: Role/task must be pre-event; wicket count alone does not establish pressure or responsibility.

Team task: Increase scoring pace while balancing dismissal risk.
Individual responsibility: Batter’s pre-event task/role, not outcome-derived label.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Pressure may exist if team task requires acceleration; high scoring alone does not prove success.
Relevant candidate observations: Required pace, balls/wickets, scoring and dismissal outcomes against baseline.
Unresolved data requirements: State rule; faced-ball classification; role-specific expectation.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — acceleration responsibility is pre-event/contextual; no numeric threshold adopted.
Dashboard handling: No numeric threshold; do not infer task from high realized scoring.

Match situation: Partnership changes after wicket or batter entry
Team task: Adapt team task to new pair and remaining resources.
Individual responsibility: Attribute outcomes to individual eligible events; partnership is context.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Shared partnership state can affect task but cannot be attributed as individual contribution.
Relevant candidate observations: Partnership score/length, strike exposure, wickets, individual outcomes.
Unresolved data requirements: Partnership/event links, strike/batter faced validity, dependency handling.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — partnership is context only; data linkage and individual attribution remain blockers.
Dashboard handling: Partnership outcomes are not automatic individual credit; show context and individual attribution separately.

Match situation: High-demand chase opportunity for lower-order batter
Team task: Pursue target with limited remaining resources and role-specific exposure.
Individual responsibility: Entry state and role may differ from top-order baseline.
Why pressure may or may not exist: May be pressure but comparison requires role-aware expectation and sufficient exposure.
Relevant candidate observations: Entry score/balls/wickets, role, eligible outcomes and prior baseline.
Unresolved data requirements: Role history, sparse opportunity, prior-only baseline and uncertainty.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — actual individual exposure and comparable role baseline required; readiness remains gated.
Dashboard handling: No top-order baseline transfer without validated comparability and sufficient evidence.

Match situation: Outcome/competition comparison across IPL and T20I
Team task: Assess whether evidence transports across competitions.
Individual responsibility: Same player may have different role and opportunity by competition.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Competition differences are not pressure states; pooling can confound response.
Relevant candidate observations: Competition-specific pressure and baseline estimates, role and coverage.
Unresolved data requirements: Comparable definitions, rules, field semantics and coverage.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — first/second innings distinct; IPL/T20I pooling remains unresolved and must not be assumed.
Dashboard handling: Competition comparison is not an independent pressure state; display IPL primary and T20I supplementary separately by default.

Scenario lineage: Added in v0.2.2 in response to METH-REV-004
Match situation: Rain interruption reduces available overs and a revised target is in force
Team task: Assess batting task using the active revised target, current score and legal balls/resources remaining immediately before the evaluated opportunity.
Individual responsibility: Batter’s verified eligible scoring and survival opportunities under the event-time state.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Task depends on the target and resources actually in force before the event; a later revision must not be retroactively applied.
Relevant candidate observations: Original target; revised target and effective time; current score; available overs/legal balls and wickets/resources in force before the event; player exposure.
Unresolved data requirements: Verified original/revised target history, event-time timestamps, active overs/resources and batter attribution. Do not infer DLS targets/resources from unavailable fields.
Authoritative disposition: CONCEPTUAL SCOPE INCLUDED — if target/overs state or event-time availability is unverified, retain UNCLASSIFIED or NOT CLASSIFIABLE and exclude from operational pressure comparisons.
Dashboard handling: Require verified active revised target/resources as of pre-event time; otherwise unclassified/not classifiable and excluded.

Match situation: Second innings / defending with opponent required pace elevated
Team task: Defend target against chase under remaining balls/resources.
Individual responsibility: Bowler’s actual eligible deliveries in assigned role/phase.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Pressure may exist from defending task; late over alone is insufficient.
Relevant candidate observations: Opponent required pace/gap, balls/wickets, target/current score, legal balls and bowler outcomes.
Unresolved data requirements: Legal-ball classification; extras/run allocation; wicket credit; time-safe state and thresholds.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — retain as second-innings defense case; containment/wicket dimensions remain separate.
Dashboard handling: Require validated state and actual eligible deliveries; containment and wicket credit separate.

Match situation: Second innings / defending with comfortable lead
Team task: Protect favorable state while opponent needs high pace.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Late innings can be low pressure if defense is comfortable; state rule needed.
Relevant candidate observations: Required pace, resources, runs conceded and eligible bowler outcomes.
Unresolved data requirements: Valid task direction, legal-ball denominator, extras and run allocation.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — retain as non-pressure/counterexample where validated state supports it.
Dashboard handling: Late innings alone is not pressure; show only if validated state rule supports counterexample.

Match situation: Close defending state with wickets and balls remaining
Team task: Manage target/current score and opponent resources.
Individual responsibility: Bowler’s assigned task and verified actual bowling opportunities and balls delivered by the bowler, distinguishing legal-ball exposure from non-legal delivery events.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Close score may indicate pressure but must be time-safe and discipline-specific.
Relevant candidate observations: Score gap, required pace, wickets/balls, role, containment and wicket credit.
Unresolved data requirements: State mapping, attribution, wicket taxonomy and exposure.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — pre-event defending task; actual exposure and attribution validation pending.
Dashboard handling: Distinguish assigned task from actual legal-ball and non-legal delivery exposure.

Team task: Limit scoring and preserve resources before chase target is known.
Individual responsibility: Bowler assigned role/phase and actual exposure.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Pressure may be tied to predeclared expected-total/innings task; existing draft does not define it.
Relevant candidate observations: Pre-event score/resource state, role, legal balls and outcome.
Unresolved data requirements: First-innings benchmark, no future target/result leakage, feasible runs.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — first-innings population separate; restricting-task benchmark remains pending.
Dashboard handling: Keep first-innings benchmark pending; no operational classification until validated and approved.

Match situation: High-demand over assigned to specialist/death role
Team task: Execute role-specific defense under match-state constraints.
Individual responsibility: Assigned over distinguished from deliveries actually bowled.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Role or death label alone does not establish pressure; state matters.
Relevant candidate observations: Assignment, actual legal balls, match state and separate outcomes.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — role context does not itself establish pressure; assigned and actual exposure distinct.
Dashboard handling: Never equate assigned over or death label with actual exposure or pressure state.

Match situation: Partnership with set batters and wickets in hand
Team task: Restrict scoring and/or create dismissal opportunity.
Individual responsibility: Individual bowler opportunity; partnership/batter state is context.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Partnership can shape task, but team partnership outcome is not individual bowler performance.
Relevant candidate observations: Batter state, wickets, score pace, containment and bowler-credit wicket.
Unresolved data requirements: Partnership linkage, legal-ball, extras and wicket credit.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — partnership/opposing batter is context, not automatic individual credit.
Dashboard handling: Team partnership outcome is not automatic bowler performance; preserve event attribution.

Match situation: Wicket event in a pressure state
Team task: Defend task and possibly take a bowler-credit wicket.
Individual responsibility: Only wickets credited to bowler under validated taxonomy.
Why pressure may or may not exist: A wicket alone does not prove successful bowling; runs, task, opportunity and credit matter.
Relevant candidate observations: Wicket type/credit, runs conceded, state, legal-ball exposure.
Authoritative disposition: OWNER-ADOPTED CONCEPT — containment and bowler-credit wicket contribution remain separate.
Dashboard handling: Display only validated bowler-credit wickets and separate containment; never equate any dismissal with bowler credit.

Match situation: Expensive over followed by next opportunity
Team task: Assess possible response/recovery in later eligible opportunity.
Individual responsibility: Next-over assignment and actual exposure; avoid conditioning only on costly prior result.
Why pressure may or may not exist: Post-hoc expensive-over selection risks regression-to-mean and role selection.
Relevant candidate observations: Sequential over outcomes, pre-event state, next assignment and match cluster.
Unresolved data requirements: Predefined event rule, selection design and sequence linkage.
Authoritative disposition: DEFERRED — post-expensive-over recovery remains a separate sequential question; no selection rule adopted.
Dashboard handling: DEFERRED; exclude from operational scoring, comparison and ranking until separately specified and approved.
